original_interpretation: Global semiconductor sales fell 8.2% in 2023 to $526.8 billion from $574.1 billion in 2022.
evidence_found: "SIA ... announced global semiconductor industry sales totaled $526.8 billion in 2023, a decrease of 8.2% compared to the 2022 total of $574.1 billion, which was the industry's highest-ever annual total." (SIA release, Feb 5, 2024, para 1)
notes: Value, unit (USD bn nominal), CY2023 and WSTS basis match. SIA's Feb 2025 release (SRC-0054) still uses $526.8bn for 2023, so no later revision found. fact/industry_body appropriate for WSTS statistics.

original_interpretation: Worldwide semiconductor sales were $248.6 billion in 2008, down 2.8% from $255.6 billion in 2007, with the steepest declines in memory where price pressure outweighed bit-shipment growth.
evidence_found: "Total sales for 2008 were $248.6 billion compared to $255.6 billion in 2007, a decrease of 2.8 percent." ... "Once again, the steepest revenue declines were in the memory sector where price pressure more than offset significant growth in total bit shipments." (SIA release, Feb 2, 2009, paras 2 and 5)
notes: Numbers and period match. The memory sentence is a quote from SIA President George Scalise, not a separate table; fine for a qualitative claim. GSR is a WSTS three-month moving average series.

original_interpretation: Worldwide semiconductor sales fell 32% in 2001 to $139 billion from $204 billion in 2000, per SIA as reported by EE Times.
evidence_found: "Worldwide semiconductor sales fell an expected 32% in 2001 ... the Semiconductor Industry Association (SIA) reported that the industry closed 2001 with sales of $139 billion, down from $204 billion in 2000." (EE Times, Bolaji Ojo, 02.04.2002, paras 1-2)
notes: Secondary (industry_press, tier 2) report of SIA data; the claim correctly attributes it. 139/204 = -31.9%, consistent with 32%. The original SIA release was not opened; for high confidence, re-point to the SIA/WSTS original if found.

original_interpretation: Nvidia's Data Center revenue rose 142% to a record $115.2 billion in fiscal 2025 (ended January 26, 2025), out of total revenue of $130.5 billion.
evidence_found: "Record full-year revenue of $130.5 billion, up 114%"; Data Center: "Fourth-quarter revenue was a record $35.6 billion ... Full-year revenue rose 142% to a record $115.2 billion." (NVIDIA Q4 FY25 release, Ex. 99.1, Feb 26, 2025, headline bullets and Highlights > Data Center); quarter "ended January 26, 2025"
notes: Fiscal year ended 2025-01-26 correctly labelled FY2025, not CY. Company-reported (company_filing exhibit) so 'fact' is acceptable for audited-basis reported results.

original_interpretation: Intel exited the DRAM business in 1985, citing falling prices, slumping demand and a supply glut, and concentrated on microprocessors (historical).
evidence_found: "As Intel explained to employees in this internal publication, falling prices, slumping demand and a glut of supply for DRAM had irrevocably depressed the market by 1985, prompting Intel to exit the business to focus on microprocessors and related products." Grove: "In retrospect, getting out of DRAMs when we did was the best business decision we ever made." (Intel timeline, 1985 'Farewell to DRAM')
notes: Company's own historical account (company_documentation); claim_type reported_claim is honest. Publication date of the timeline page unknown.

original_interpretation: On March 23, 2021 Intel announced its 'IDM 2.0' strategy combining its internal factory network, expanded use of third-party foundry capacity, and a new standalone Intel Foundry Services unit, plus about $20 billion for two new fabs in Arizona.
evidence_found: "Announcing manufacturing expansion plans; beginning with ~$20 billion investment to build two new fabs in Arizona"; "2. Expanded use of third-party foundry capacity"; "Intel is establishing a new standalone business unit, Intel Foundry Services (IFS)"; "This build-out represents an investment of approximately $20 billion" (Intel Ex. 99.1, March 23, 2021, News Highlights and p. 2-3)
notes: All three IDM 2.0 elements and the ~$20bn Arizona figure are in the release. The $20bn is an announced plan (forward-looking), not spend; metric population says 'announced capital investment', which is correct.

original_interpretation: On August 22, 2025 Intel announced the US government would buy 433.3 million Intel shares at $20.47 (a 9.9% stake, $8.9 billion), funded by $5.7 billion of unpaid CHIPS Act grants and $3.2 billion from the Secure Enclave program.
evidence_found: "the government agrees to purchase 433.3 million primary shares of Intel common stock at a price of $20.47 per share, equivalent to a 9.9 percent stake"; "funded by the remaining $5.7 billion in grants previously awarded, but not yet paid ... under the U.S. CHIPS and Science Act and $3.2 billion awarded ... as part of the Secure Enclave program" (Intel release, Aug 22, 2025)
notes: reported_claim/company_documentation appropriate. Closing 8-K (SRC-0316) shows the structure: on Aug 27, 2025 Intel received $5.695bn and issued 274,583,000 shares plus a warrant for up to 240,516,150 shares, with 158,740,000 shares in escrow released as Secure Enclave disbursements arrive. $20.47 is the blended price ($8.87bn / 433.3m); 8-K Item 1.01 implies $20.74 (issued) and $20.00 (escrowed). Already captured by CLM-0964/CLM-0969.

original_interpretation: The Fabless Semiconductor Association was founded in 1994 and renamed itself the Global Semiconductor Alliance on December 3, 2007, saying it had met its original goal of proliferating the fabless business model.
evidence_found: "December 3, 2007 – The Fabless Semiconductor Association is dropping the 'fabless' from its name and going 'global,' claiming that it's met original goals to proliferate the fabless business model and now must expand its agenda to address challenges through the entire chipmaking supply chain. Formed in 1994, the FSA has swelled to 500 members in 25 countries" (Solid State Technology, Dec 3, 2007, paras 1-2)
notes: industry_press (tier 2) reporting the association's own statement; the 'met its goals' part is the association's self-description, correctly framed with 'saying'. Dec 3, 2007 is the announcement/article date.

original_interpretation: Nvidia's proposed $40 billion acquisition of Arm was abandoned in February 2022 after the FTC sued to block it in December 2021, citing harm to competition in ADAS processors, DPU SmartNICs and Arm-based cloud CPUs.
evidence_found: FTC statement Feb 14, 2022: "Nvidia this week announced that it would abandon its acquisition of Arm." "On December 2, 2021, the Commission voted to file an administrative complaint to block the proposed transaction." Harm alleged in "(1) processors for High-Level Advanced Driver Assistance Systems for passenger cars; (2) DPU SmartNICs ...; and (3) Arm-based CPUs for cloud computing service providers." Related release: "FTC Sues to Block $40 Billion Semiconductor Chip Merger"
notes: Opened via direct HTML (web_extract elided the middle). 'Sued' = administrative complaint, not federal court suit; claim wording 'sued to block' matches FTC's own headline. $40bn appears in the linked FTC release title, not in this statement's body.

original_interpretation: On October 7, 2008 AMD and Abu Dhabi's ATIC announced they would move AMD's manufacturing operations, including its Dresden fabs, into a jointly owned manufacturing company (initially 'The Foundry Company', later GlobalFoundries), with AMD holding 44.4% and ATIC 55.6%.
evidence_found: "The new global company, to be temporarily called 'The Foundry Company'"; "AMD will contribute to The Foundry Company its manufacturing facilities, including two fabrication facilities in Dresden, Germany"; "AMD will own 44.4 percent and ATIC will own 55.6 percent of The Foundry Company's fully-converted common stock upon its formation." (Mubadala release, 07 Oct 2008)
notes: Board seats and voting rights were equal; 44.4/55.6 is 'on a fully converted to common basis', and ATIC's economic share was set to rise over time. The cited release does not contain the GlobalFoundries name. Added a new claim citing AMD's Apr 21, 2009 release (Ex. 99.1): the transaction closed 'creating GLOBALFOUNDRIES', consolidated as of March 2, 2009.
correction: Ownership split is on a fully-converted basis with equal board/voting rights. The 'later GlobalFoundries' part is not in SRC-0064; it is supported by AMD's Q1 2009 release (new source in this batch).

original_interpretation: Samsung developed a 64Kb DRAM in 1983, achieved the world's largest DRAM market share in 1992 and the largest memory market share in 1993.
evidence_found: "1983 · Initiates VLSI business · Develops 64Kb DRAM"; "1992 · Develops industry's first 64Mb DRAM · Achieves world's largest DRAM market share"; "1993 · Opens industry's first 200mm fabrication line (Line 5) · Achieves world's largest memory market share" (Samsung Semiconductor Newsroom, About Us, history timeline)
notes: Company self-history; reported_claim is the correct type. Market-share rankings are not independently sourced here.

original_interpretation: Between 1978 and 1986 the US share of the DRAM market fell from about 70% to 20% while the Japanese share rose from under 30% to about 75% (historical estimate).
evidence_found: "Spectacular success was achieved in DRAMS: the U.S. market share plummeted from 70 to 20 percent between 1978 and 1986 as the Japanese share jumped from under 30 to about 75 percent." (Irwin 1996, NBER chapter, section 1.3 'Semiconductor Competition from Japan')
notes: Quote matches exactly. Irwin does not say whether this is the world or US DRAM market; metric geography 'World' is the researcher's reading, plausible because USITC ID-062 (p. 7) restates it as Japanese firms' market share 'from less than 30 percent to nearly 75 percent between 1978 and 1986'. Underlying data is in a footnote not rendered. Historical and correctly labelled estimate.

original_interpretation: In the 1985 downturn DRAM prices collapsed and the memory-chip market contracted about 60%, and every US merchant producer except Texas Instruments and Micron was pushed out of the DRAM market (historical).
evidence_found: "The industry recession of 1985 was extremely severe ... Prices collapsed and the memory-chip market contracted 60 percent. Merchant firms racked up unprecedented losses. ... Every U.S. merchant producer was pushed out of the DRAM market except Texas Instruments and Micron." (Irwin 1996, section 1.4.1 'Dumping')
notes: The text ties the 60% contraction to the 1985 recession, so metric period can be '1985' rather than 'c.1985'. Underlying data source is a footnote not rendered in the extract.

original_interpretation: Higher DRAM prices after the 1986 US-Japan agreement accelerated the entry of South Korean firms not covered by the restraint (historical, late 1980s).
evidence_found: "Higher DRAM prices accelerated the entry of South Korean firms not covered by the restraint. Only two U.S. merchant firms (TI and Micron) remained in the DRAM market to benefit from the antidumping actions." (Irwin 1996, section on effects of the 1986 Arrangement; context discusses 1988 profits)
notes: Causal analysis by an academic economist, correctly typed estimate/analysis. USITC ID-062 (p. 11) says something similar: Korean firms expanded as Japanese firms cut output under the US settlement.

original_interpretation: In June 2014 China released its National IC Industry Development Guidelines and in September 2014 launched the National IC Industry Investment Fund ('Big Fund') to fund both outbound acquisitions and inbound investment.
evidence_found: "In June 2014, the Chinese Government released Guidelines to Promote National Integrated Circuit Industry (National IC Plan)." "Since it was launched in September 2014, the National IC Fund has engaged in a two-pronged strategy. On one hand, it funds outbound FDI to acquire foreign companies. On the other, it provides funds to facilitate inbound FDI" (VerWey, USITC JICE July 2019, p. 13)
notes: Page and wording confirmed from the full PDF text. USITC staff paper (government source, author's views).

original_interpretation: A 2019 USITC staff paper described the National IC Fund plus provincial and municipal IC funds as targeting $150 billion, with the national fund at roughly $21 billion and local funds over $80 billion raised as of 2017.
evidence_found: p. 13: National IC Fund "Endowed with $150 billion in funds from the central and provincial governments"; "The SIA estimated that, as of 2017, while the National IC Fund had secured roughly $21 billion in funding, provincial and municipal IC-related funds have raised over $80 billion and are well on their way to reaching the goal of $150 billion." (fn 71: adapted from USTR Section 301 Report)
notes: The researcher's evidence partly came from a fetch summary; it is now confirmed verbatim. The paper is internally inconsistent: it calls the national fund 'endowed with $150 billion' but then says it had secured ~$21bn. Official phase-1 registered capital was 138.7 bn yuan (CLM-0132). Added a superseding claim with the correct attribution.
correction: The $21bn/$80bn figures are an SIA estimate (via USTR) quoted by the USITC paper, not the author's own compilation, and $150bn is described as a goal; the paper also inconsistently says the national fund was 'endowed with $150 billion'.

original_interpretation: China has consumed more chips than the rest of the world combined every year since 2012, per a 2019 USITC staff paper.
evidence_found: "As figure 2 shows, China has consumed more chips than the rest of the world combined every year since 2012." (VerWey 2019, p. 6; Figure 2 'Worldwide semiconductor consumption market by region, 2003–16', p. 7, source PwC 2017)
notes: The sentence is on p. 6, not p. 7 (Figure 2 is on p. 7). Chart data is PwC and runs only to 2016; chart values not checked. The same page explains that demand comes from goods China makes for export as well as domestic use, so 'consumption' means chips shipped into China, including for re-exported devices (the researcher's note is correct).

original_interpretation: China's Integrated Circuit Industry Investment Fund had registered capital of 138.7 billion yuan in phase 1 (2014), 204 billion yuan in phase 2 (2019) and 344 billion yuan in phase 3 (established May 2024).
evidence_found: "the fund, which was officially established on Friday with a registered capital of 344 billion yuan, according to the National Enterprise Credit Information Publicity System"; "The first phase of the Big Fund was established in 2014 with a registered capital of 138.7 billion yuan and the second phase followed in 2019 with 204 billion yuan." (english.gov.cn, May 29, 2024)
notes: The page is a China Daily article republished on the State Council's English site ('Updated: May 29, 2024 ... China Daily'), quoting the government credit registry. Arguably state media rather than a government publication, but the registry figures are official. 'Friday' = 24 May 2024.

original_interpretation: Japanese DRAM maker Elpida filed for corporate reorganization at the Tokyo District Court on February 27, 2012, and on July 2, 2012 Micron signed a sponsor agreement to acquire it for total consideration of 200 billion yen.
evidence_found: "Elpida filed a petition for commencement of Corporate Reorganization Proceedings with the Tokyo District Court under the Corporate Reorganization Act of Japan on Feb. 27, 2012."; "Under the agreement, 200 billion Yen (approximately USD $2.5 billion assuming 80 Yen/USD) total consideration, less certain reorganization proceeding expenses, will be used to satisfy the reorganization claims" (Micron Ex. 99.1, July 2, 2012)
notes: Split: 60bn yen cash at closing for 100% of equity plus 140bn yen in installments through 2019. 'Acquire it for total consideration of 200 billion yen' is a fair summary; the total is gross of reorganization expenses.

original_interpretation: Four Taiwanese companies, led by TSMC, together accounted for 68.7% of global foundry services revenue in Q1 2023 (per TrendForce, cited by USITC).
evidence_found: "Four Taiwanese companies, including Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC)—the world's largest foundry, were ranked among the world's top ten foundries, together accounting for 68.7 percent of global foundry services revenue in the first quarter of 2023." (USITC working paper 2023-11-A, p. 13, fn 44: TrendForce, June 12, 2023)
notes: A research-firm estimate cited by a government paper; claim_type estimate and attribution are correct. The figure covers a single quarter (1Q23), so later TrendForce quarters do not make it outdated.

original_interpretation: On July 1, 2019 Japan announced restrictions on exports to South Korea of key semiconductor materials (fluorinated polyimide, photoresist, hydrogen fluoride), and on August 2, 2019 removed Korea from its export 'white list'.
evidence_found: p. 4: "On July 1, 2019, Japan announced that it would restrict exports of certain key semiconductor manufacturing materials to Korea. These materials—hydrogen fluoride, fluorinated polyimides, and photoresist/resist"; p. 5: "Japan also removed Korea from its 'white list' countries" (fn 20: METI, 'The Cabinet Approved partial Amendment to the Export Trade Control Order,' August 2, 2019). EY (29 Aug 2019): removal approved 2 Aug, "officially removed from the list on 28 August".
notes: The source does not itself date the removal to Aug 2; that date comes from its footnote citing the Cabinet approval. METI's English release URL now returns 'Page Not Found', so the Aug 28 effective date rests on EY (tier 3). Added a superseding claim with both dates.
correction: On August 2, 2019 Japan's Cabinet approved removing Korea from the white list (Group A); the removal took effect on August 28, 2019.

original_interpretation: Japanese media cited by the USITC reported Japan produced about 90% of global photoresists and about 70% of hydrogen fluoride used for etching (circa 2019).
evidence_found: "Japanese media reports that Japan produces approximately 90 percent of global photoresists, and over 90 percent of 2018 Korean photoresist imports originated from Japan." (p. 18); "Japanese media reports that Japan produces 70 percent of the HF used for etching globally." (p. 14, fn 54: Reuters factbox, July 2, 2019) (USITC ID-062, Oct 2019)
notes: Read from the full PDF text via a reader proxy (r.jina.ai) because usitc.gov returned 403 to direct downloads. Photoresist passage is on p. 18 (not p. 19). Caveat: the 70% covers high-purity HF for etching only; the same page says Japan makes 'less than five percent of global HF' overall. The source is second-hand media, so evidentiary weight is low, as the researcher noted.

original_interpretation: The Netherlands' national export control measure on advanced semiconductor manufacturing equipment took effect on September 1, 2023 and was expanded on September 7, 2024 to cover more deep-ultraviolet lithography equipment, citing security reasons.
evidence_found: "As of 7 September 2024, the national export control measure applicable to advanced semiconductor manufacturing equipment will be expanded, making more types of equipment subject to a national authorisation requirement." "...existing national export control rules that have been in force since 1 September 2023. They apply to ... deep ultraviolet lithography equipment." Klever: "I've made this decision for reasons of security." (Government.nl, 06-09-2024)
notes: Accurate for the two events named. Later change: a second amendment took effect 1 April 2025 and added 'specific measuring and inspection equipment' (Government.nl, 15-01-2025, SRC-0132; captured as CLM-0338). The measure is a licence requirement assessed case by case, 'not an export ban'.

original_interpretation: ASML emerged as the sole supplier of EUV lithography machines, and EUV entered commercial production in 2019 when the first EUV-enabled consumer electronics were released (per CSET, 2024).
evidence_found: "The Dutch company ASML has emerged as the sole supplier of EUV machines, winning a 30-year race that granted the company a monopoly on selling the tool essential for fabricating leading-edge semiconductors."; "In 2019, when the first commercial electronics enabled by EUV were released, the technology was hailed as 'the machine that saved Moore's Law.'" (CSET, VerWey, July 2024, Executive Summary)
notes: Academic think-tank (tier 2) characterisation; claim correctly attributes it to CSET.

original_interpretation: On May 28, 2015 Avago Technologies agreed to acquire Broadcom Corporation in a transaction valued at $37 billion, creating a combined company with about $15 billion in annual revenue (consolidation wave of the mid-2010s).
evidence_found: "Avago Technologies to Acquire Broadcom for $37 Billion"; "Based on Avago's closing share price as of May 27, 2015, the implied value of the total transaction consideration for Broadcom is $37 billion."; "combined annual revenues of approximately $15 billion"; "Creates the world's leading diversified communications semiconductor company" (Ex. 99.1, May 28, 2015)
notes: The $37bn is implied value at announcement ($17bn cash plus stock worth ~$20bn), as the metric population says. The 'consolidation wave' framing is the researcher's context, not from the release.

original_interpretation: Arm was established in 1990 as a joint venture between Acorn Computers, Apple Computer and VLSI Technology, and earns licence fees plus per-unit royalties on chips made by others rather than manufacturing chips itself.
evidence_found: "Established in 1990, Arm began as a joint venture between Acorn Computers, Apple Computer, and VLSI Technology." (Our Journey History); "Our customers license our products for a fee ... Once a chip has been designed and manufactured with our products, we receive a per-unit royalty on substantially all chips shipped." (Our Business Model and Customers) (Arm 424B4, Sept 2023)
notes: Accurate as of the 2023 prospectus. Newer development: Arm's May 2026 shareholder letter (SRC-0514) says it launched 'the Arm AGI CPU, the first Arm-designed chip for the data center' / 'our first production silicon product', so from FY2026 Arm also sells its own chips, while still not running fabs. The atlas should not describe Arm as purely licence-plus-royalty after 2026.

original_interpretation: Arm stated in its 2023 IPO prospectus that more than 250 billion Arm-based chips had shipped cumulatively.
evidence_found: Prospectus: "more than 250 billion chips, cumulatively, powering everything from the tiniest of sensors to the most powerful supercomputers" (424B4, Prospectus Summary). Newer: "With over 350 billion chips shipped and over 22 million developers" (Arm 6-K, Shareholder Letter, May 6, 2026); Q3 FYE26 deck (Feb 2026): "+325bn Arm-based chips shipped ... since 1990".
notes: The prospectus statement is accurate historically, but the figure is superseded. Added a new claim (supersedes CLM-0111) citing the May 2026 shareholder letter. Arm-reported; method not disclosed.
correction: Arm reported over 350 billion cumulative Arm-based chips shipped as of its May 2026 FYE26 results (up from >250bn in the 2023 prospectus).

original_interpretation: On April 1, 2025 the US Commerce Secretary initiated a Section 232 national-security investigation into imports of semiconductors, semiconductor manufacturing equipment and their derivative products.
evidence_found: "On April 1, 2025, the Secretary of Commerce initiated an investigation under section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act (19 U.S.C. 1862) to determine the effects on national security of imports of semiconductors, semiconductor manufacturing equipment, and their derivative products." (90 FR 15950, FR Doc. 2025-06591, Apr 16, 2025, Background)
notes: Quote taken from the document's full-text XML on federalregister.gov, since the HTML extract was elided. BIS notice; comments closed 05/07/2025. The claim concerns initiation only; later 232 outcomes are covered elsewhere.

original_interpretation: Interpretation: the industry's value capture shifted from vertically integrated firms toward specialists - fabless designers, pure-play foundries and IP licensors - between the mid-1980s and 2010s, as seen in ITRI's foundry spin-offs, UMC's 1995 switch to pure-play, AMD's 2008 fab separation and the fabless association's 2007 statement that its goals were met.
evidence_found: Underlying sources re-opened: FSA renamed GSA after saying it had 'met original goals to proliferate the fabless business model' (SRC-0062); AMD put its fabs into a separate manufacturing company to 'focus our efforts on design' (SRC-0064); Arm licenses designs and collects per-unit royalties (SRC-0075). UMC/TSMC/ITRI claims (CLM-0104-0107) were not checked in this run.
notes: The cited cases do show the industry structure moving toward specialised fabless, foundry and IP models from the late 1980s to 2010s. But 'value capture shifted' is a claim about revenue or profit shares, and none of the named claims measures that (the batch's own unknown CLM-0152 admits there is no fabless-share series). Evidence field 'claims c18-c26' is vague. The interpretation needs a share series to be fully supported.
correction: Supported as a shift in business models toward specialists; 'value capture' is not shown, since no revenue or profit-share series is cited.

original_interpretation: Interpretation: each major trade/policy shift has been triggered by a perceived competitive or security threat from another region - Japan in the 1980s (1986 Arrangement, 1987 sanctions, SEMATECH) and China from 2014 onwards (Big Fund, then US entity listings 2019 and export controls 2022, followed by Dutch controls 2023) - with the 2020-22 shortage adding supply-security arguments for subsidies (CHIPS Act 2022, EU Chips Act 2023).
evidence_found: Counter-example in SRC-0071 p. 4: Japan's July 2019 controls on Korea — "Analysts have traced the origins of these actions as a part of a longstanding dispute between the two countries concerning reparations for forced Korean labor during Japan's colonial-WWII period." Dutch 2024 expansion justified 'for reasons of security' (SRC-0072); China 2014 IC Plan aimed at catch-up/self-sufficiency (SRC-0067 p. 12-13).
notes: The pattern fits the US-Japan 1980s and US/allies-China 2019-2024 episodes, and the shortage-to-subsidy link is plausible. But 'each major trade/policy shift' is too strong: the 2019 Japan-Korea controls (in this batch) came from a historical-reparations dispute, not a competitive or security threat, and China's 2014 plan is framed as catch-up and self-sufficiency, not a reaction to another region's threat. Several underlying claims (CLM-0099, 0100, 0102, 0135, 0138, 0139, 0141) were not checked in this run.
correction: Replace 'each' with 'most': the 2019 Japan-Korea export controls were tied to a forced-labour reparations dispute, not a competitive or security threat.

original_interpretation: Inference: memory is the most cyclical segment historically - memory drove the 1985 collapse, the steepest declines in 2008, and the largest swing up in 2024 (+78.9%).
evidence_found: 1985: "Prices collapsed and the memory-chip market contracted 60 percent" (SRC-0066); 2008: "the steepest revenue declines were in the memory sector" (SRC-0056); 2024: "Memory products were second in terms of sales, increasing by 78.9% in 2024 to a total of $165.1 billion. DRAM products ... recorded an 82.6% sales increase, the largest percentage growth of any product category in 2024." (SRC-0054)
notes: All three data points check out. But three episodes do not show memory is the 'most cyclical' segment: no volatility series across segments was compiled, as the researcher admits. In 2024 the largest-growth category SIA names is DRAM (+82.6%), a subset of memory. Treat as a plausible hypothesis pending a segment time series (e.g. WSTS by product).
correction: The data points are correct, but 'most cyclical' needs a cross-segment volatility series; in 2024 SIA names DRAM (+82.6%) as the fastest-growing category.

original_interpretation: Inference: the AI-driven demand shift is visible in primary data by 2024-2025 - Nvidia Data Center revenue of $115.2bn in FY2025, HPC reaching 58% of TSMC revenue in 2025, and logic plus memory driving 25.6% industry growth in 2025.
evidence_found: Nvidia FY2025: Data Center "Full-year revenue rose 142% to a record $115.2 billion" (SRC-0058); TSMC 4Q25 Management Report: "Net Revenue by Platform 2025 2024 High Performance Computing 58% 51%" (SRC-0024); SIA Feb 6, 2026: sales "$791.7 billion in 2025, an increase of 25.6%"; "Logic and memory products saw largest growth" (logic +39.9% to $301.9bn; memory +34.8% to $223.1bn) (SRC-0007)
notes: All figures verified against primary documents. The AI attribution is not in these sources: TSMC's HPC platform includes non-AI CPUs and other chips; SIA mentions AI only in a forward-looking CEO quote; only Nvidia's Data Center line is clearly AI-led. (SIA release typo: memory 'increasing by 34.8% in 2024' refers to 2025.)
correction: Numbers verified; the claim that the growth is AI-driven is the companies' framing and is not measured by these sources.
